items.title: Carl and Laura Lentz Speak Out About ‘Darkness,’ Hope Years After Scandal — and Offer a Path for ‘Overcoming Infidelity’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's almost like the most defeating, shame spiral you could ever imagine."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Carl Lentz was a preacher who seemed to have it all, until a moral failure forced him out as lead pastor of Hillsong NYC/East Coast.

His shocking firing rocked the evangelical world. Six years later, Lentz is sharing his healing journey. He and his wife, Laura, have a new book, “Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help You Heal the Hurt,” which helps guide people through the process.

Carl told CBN News they wrote the book to share their perspective and help others “make a dark season lighter.”

“We wanted to help people as fast as we could because we don’t think that you can get through it without help,” he said. “And we wanted to put as much as we’ve learned, and learn, and are currently learning, on paper.”

Carl said they hope to redeem what happened by helping others navigate similar struggles. Laura said she has received multitudes of messages from people over the past few years asking questions and seeking assistance.

Her experience has equipped her to guide others through the unthinkable, especially considering the very public nature of Carl’s affair — something that forced her to deal with other layers people in similar situations might not face.

“Finding out that you’ve been betrayed is really hard,” she said. “It’s awful. I wouldn’t wish it on anyone, but the public part was really hard, because you have extra voices coming at you, and giving their opinions, and their hate, and what they think, that’s confusing as well, and hurtful.”

Ultimately, Laura said it was a “very lonely road,” but one she was able to navigate. She said “it was very dark” before she found out what was truly happening in her husband’s life.

“A week before everything came out, I was in the shower just crying out to God. I was just like, God, whatever’s going on in him, just get it out,” she said. “You could see it in his eyes. His eyes had no life left. … I would look in his eyes and .. it was just darkness there.”

Once the truth came out, everything made more sense.

For Carl, the public piece of the puzzle was obviously quite intense. At first, despite the pain and sorrow, he said there was a relief that the truth had been revealed. That left him thinking, “Well, my life’s over, and I’m just gonna try to do what I can, patch this up, and I’m just gonna go off into a hole.” The journey from there wasn’t easy.

“It’s almost like the most defeating, shame spiral you could ever imagine,” Carl said. “In regard to the humiliation, I think I was not in a good place in my soul, so I didn’t care.”

He didn’t realize at the time, due to the state of his heart, mind, and soul, the impact the ordeal would have on his family.

“I wasn’t prepared for the impact on my family,” he said. “I just wasn’t. That’s the honest truth. … I didn’t care about what people were saying. It was more about the impact on my kids and my wife.”

Looking back, Carl said he truly believes he wasn’t well at the time of his moral failing. He said he faced an “avalanche of despair” in the wake of the chaos.

“I don’t even feel like I was in my right mind, and a part of me is grateful, because I feel like … if you’re living with that kind of duplicity and you can function, I don’t know what the future is for somebody like that,” he said. “There was help I could have gotten, there were people I could have talked to, there were better avenues.”

The natural question many have for the Lentzes: what led them to stay together after such a horrific public journey?

“I got some advice early on, which was really helpful for me, not to make any big decisions right away, any big life-altering decisions,” Laura said. “Just to take it a day at a time.”

Meanwhile, Carl went on a healing journey to address the past and present issues he was experiencing, including past childhood abuse. Laura said it was not an excuse for behavior but was helpful to understanding him.

“It … just kind of gave me a little bit more context as to how broken he was and …. hurt was inside of him that he’s never talked about,” she said, noting that she didn’t want to leave in those early moments and instead took the advice to take it day by day.

Carl also reflected on seeing help and healing his marriage.

“I got some immediate help and uncovered some things that, again, for anybody listening, when you explain context, it’s never an excuse,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what the context is. Unacceptable choices were made by me.”

Ultimately, Carl was able to ask some important questions about how he ended up in that position and why he made the choices he did. As for church accountability, Carl didn’t place blame on anyone other than himself.

“I had a great system around me,” he said. “Accountability is so worthless if people are not honest with themselves.”

The couple hopes that being open and candid and writing “Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations to Help You Heal the Hurt” will help others facing similar circumstances.

“We’re just doing what God’s called us to do in this chapter,” Carl said. “We’ve written a book, and we want to tell people about it and get the word out, and if someone wants to talk, we’re gonna talk.”

items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Bring Your Bible and Your Shotgun: Meet the Most Florida Church Plant Ever
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers. The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Black
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Sunday services at TruLife Church of Ocala’s newest campus come with a soundtrack of shotguns going off in the distance. Some attendees bring their own and check them at a rack by the door, the way other congregations check strollers.

The campus is called BlackJack, like the range it meets at: Blackjack Sporting Clays, a shooting facility in Sumterville, Fla. The facility’s owners came up with the idea and asked pastor Michael Kirby about starting a church plant on the property. Kirby has a handy comparison for the place, which has four courses and a cart. “You rent a golf cart and you drive around and shoot clays at all the different posts,” he said. “It’s like playing golf, but you’re playing with a shotgun.” So it’s golf, but the clubs go off.

The sanctuary, loosely speaking, is a pavilion enclosed in thick, clear plastic, with mobile air conditioners keeping the cool air in and the wooded views visible. An 80-inch TV and a full sound system play Kirby’s prerecorded sermon three weeks a month, so three Sundays out of four the preacher arrives by screen. He or another TruLife pastor preaches live once a month, and Kirby’s daughter-in-law, Taylor Kirby, leads worship. Seating is about 40.

The church held a soft opening a couple of months ago and had its official launch on Sunday, Oct. 25, with Kirby preaching and a picnic lunch afterward. The day before, during a national competitive shooting event at the facility, volunteers handed out flyers and went door to door in the neighborhood, which is outreach with an unusually loud backdrop.

The target audience is the person who came to shoot. “We are hoping to attract unchurched people who are coming to BlackJack to do some shooting,” Kirby said. “Maybe they wouldn’t want to go to your typical church, but they decide they could go over here under the pavilion and hang out.” Evangelism by proximity, in other words: set up next to the people with the shotguns and hope they wander over.

Some of them already have noticed the music. Kirby says shooters have told him they can hear the worship from the service, and he is counting on it. “They might not come inside yet, but they’ll be out there worshipping in the middle of the grass,” he said. The worship set, it turns out, doubles as the range’s ambient soundtrack.

items.title: Evangelization, Dialogue, Conversion, and Cardinal Vesco
items.author: Dr. Richard DeClue
items.summary:
Dr. Richard DeClue

Disagreements can be precisely the beginning of a conversation. That’s what interreligious dialogue is all about.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

Cardinal Jean-Paul Vesco, Archbishop of Algiers, is caught between the proverbial rock and hard place of legal and religious tensions. In a May 27, 2009, report entitled “Algeria bans Muslims from learning about Christianity,” the website of the European Centre for Law & Justice notes:

The Algerian parliament has approved a law banning the call to embrace other religions than Islam.

This Law states to jail anyone “trying to call on a Muslim to embrace another religion,” in remarks to the Christianizing (evangelize) campaigns taking place in the country.

[ . . . ]

The ratified law stated to sentence imprisonment for two to five years and a fee between 5 to 10 thousand EURO against “anyone urging or forcing or tempting, to convert a Muslim to another religion.”

As a former lawyer for seven years and as a Cardinal Archbishop from the Dominican Order, His Eminence has tremendous experience in both law and religion. I do not envy his situation; he must navigate a precarious environment in which the call to evangelize is threatened with legal punishments.

In this way, Cardinal Vesco finds himself in circumstances not unlike those of the Apostles and early Church Fathers, many of whom were martyred precisely because of their missionary efforts.

In the Acts of the Apostles, we read that King Herod “had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword” (12:2). He then had Peter arrested as well (12:3). This wasn’t the first time Peter and the Apostles had been imprisoned. Already once before, the high priest and Sadducees “arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison” (Acts 5:18). Both times, there were miraculous escapes through angelic intervention.

During the first prison break, “an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and said, ‘Go, stand in the temple and tell the people the whole message about this life.’ When they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and went on with their teaching” (5:19–20).

So, immediately after escaping, Peter and the Apostles heeded the divine command to continue the proclamation of the Gospel precisely in a place where they would easily be found and recaptured, which is exactly what happened.

The high priest then addressed the Apostles with words similar to the Algerian Law: “‘We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching’” (5:28). Peter’s response to this interrogation is telling: “‘We must obey God rather than any human authority’” (5:29). St. Peter was eventually martyred for his refusal to bow to secular authority, as were numerous other martyrs during the first few hundred years of Christianity’s persecution by Roman emperors.

Christian Martyrdom has not ceased. As Robert Royal reports in an article published on All Souls Day, “Within just one week, two massacres of Christians took place that went almost unnoticed. In Jordan, nine Christians were killed and dozens more wounded during a funeral procession at St. George’s Orthodox Church. And in Ethiopia, sixty Christians were murdered in two separate incidents by gunmen who went house to house, hunting them down and burning twenty of their homes along the way.”

The threat, especially in Christian-minority lands, is real. Those of us who live in places of relative safety ought not be over-confident that we would be more courageous in the face of such persecution than those whom we criticize. For, alongside the countless martyrs in the early Church, there were also many who capitulated to the demands of the political power of their day.

No one is questioning the difficulty of Cardinal Vesco’s situation and the weight he must feel regarding the safety of his flock. But the question remains: Were Cardinal Vesco’s now famous remarks—made to a Belgian, not an Algerian outlet—an authentic Catholic view regarding evangelization and conversion? Whether he has said these words under duress is not the issue; the issue is their truthfulness.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

In an interview with Christophe Herinckx of CathoBel, Cardinal Vesco made the following remarks about the Church in Algeria:

Another challenge, since Algerian independence, has been to be, as much as possible, a Church that participates fully in civic life, one that is woven into the life of the country. Above all, we must not be a community closed in on itself. That would not be the Church. We are the Church of this people. Not a proselytizing Church, not a Church that is there to convert, but a Church that aspires to be one of the constituent parts of this people.

The dispute over the cardinal’s remarks center around two key terms: “proselytizing” and “convert.” The former can be understood in one of two ways. In the first way, proselytizing is distinct from proper evangelization, insofar as it uses coercive techniques, whether threat of punishment or promises of earthly goods. In another sense, it is at least a partial-synonym for evangelization and simply means any attempt to convert someone from one religion to another, including through proclamation or attempts to convince through rational discussion. Despite what Christophe Herinckx thinks, Bishop Barron is not confused about this term. Today, proselytizing is more often used in distinction from evangelization, and Bishop Barron explicitly cites this difference in his criticism of Cardinal Vesco’s words.

It is Cardinal Vesco’s equation of “a proselytizing Church” and “a Church that is there to convert” that Bishop Barron contests. Additionally, Cardinal Vesco removed all doubt about his denial of the call to evangelize. In his own response to Bishop Barron on a Facebook post, Cardinal Vesco plainly said, “Yes, I believe that believers of the three monotheisms [Christianity, Judaism, and Islam] have something better to do than trying to convert one another.”

The Great Commission consists precisely in making disciples of all nations and baptizing them into Christ and his Church (Matt 28:19). The Apostles carried this out to both Jews and Gentiles alike. All nations means all nations and peoples, none excepted.

Some have come to the cardinal’s defense by claiming that it isn’t our job to convert; it’s the Holy Spirit who converts. That’s only partially true, and it is ultimately irrelevant. Let me explain.

Yes, in the midst of our proclamation of the Gospel, ultimately, the Holy Spirit is the one who offers the gift of faith by which people can repent and believe in the Gospel. But that doesn’t excuse us from the command to proclaim the gospel, which is precisely the matter under dispute. Secondly, the Holy Spirit works in and through proclamation.

It is fitting, in this context, to cite someone who actually did convert and was also the greatest of evangelizers: St. Paul. What does he have to say about all this?

Regarding whether or not he should evangelize, St. Paul says, “An obligation is laid on me, and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel!” (1 Cor 9:16b). With respect to the faithfuls’ role in bringing souls to Christ, he does not say “don’t worry about it, the Holy Spirit has it covered.” Quite to the contrary, he states, “But how are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim? And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? . . . faith comes from what is heard” (Rom 10:14–15, 17).

St. Paul was a convert from one monotheism to another (pace, Cardinal Vesco), and he sought to convert his fellow Jews as well as Gentiles to the truth of faith in Christ. He conducted this evangelization in the midst of a religious and political situation that wanted to—and did—kill him for it.

No law forbidding proclamation of the gospel is valid. As Dignitatis Humanae says to nations that try to stop the Church from evangelizing, “In the face of government the Church claims freedom for herself in her character as a spiritual authority, established by Christ the Lord, upon which there rests, by divine mandate, the duty of going out into the whole world and preaching the Gospel to every creature” (13).

I not only disagree with Cardinal Vesco’s words cited above, I also have a problem with the less-discussed rationale he offers for his outlook. In the original interview, he stated, “In the monotheistic religions, proselytism is a poison because it implies considering the other person’s religion to be false. When I have a Muslim in front of me who says, ‘You’re a good person, but your religion is worthless,’ that brings the dialogue to an end. Suddenly we are no longer of the same world; we no longer belong to the same humanity. We have to fight against that.”

We’ve already addressed the problem with how the word proselytism is being used above, so I won’t rehash that. That aside, I do not agree with his assessment. Cardinal Vesco is saying if I disagree with someone else, then we are “no longer of the same world” and “no longer belong to the same humanity.” That, to me, is patently false. I can think someone is wrong about something, including religious beliefs, without thinking we don’t share the same humanity. 

Also, I don’t think such statements about disagreements have to be the end of the discussion. They can be precisely the beginning of a conversation. That’s what interreligious dialogue is all about. As one of my former professors, Fr. Harvey Egan, SJ, once told me, “It is not dialogue if you give up your position from the start.” In other words, pretending you agree when you don’t is not authentic dialogue.

The whole purpose of dialogue is predicated on a mutual desire to help one another come to a better grasp of the truth. The fact that we already disagree is precisely that: a fact. Islam does think Christianity is wrong about Christ; Christians think Islam is wrong about Christ. No amount of pretending we don’t think the other is wrong about these beliefs will change that fact. At least the hypothetical Muslim the cardinal speaks of is being honest, and honesty about our differences is the beginning of authentic dialogue. The scenario shouldn’t be: “I think you are wrong, so let’s not talk.” It should be: “We both think the other’s position is mistaken—let’s discuss.” It is the willingness to rationally discuss in the face of disagreement that manifests our recognition of the other’s dignity. There is nothing dignified about burying our heads in the sand and refusing to discuss our differences openly and honestly.

Honesty about one’s beliefs, especially when they contradict those of the other, are necessary for dialogue, and so is the prior commitment to the truth. In his book The Nature and Mission of Theology, Joseph Ratzinger uses St. Augustine’s own conversion experience as a powerful example. He writes, “Augustine concludes that the community of friends was capable of mutual listening and understanding because all of them together heeded the interior master, the truth. . . . Dialogue without this interior obedient listening to the truth would be nothing more than a discussion among the deaf” (34). As I commented in the The New Apologetics, “If there is no truth which both parties are committed to seeking and to obeying, then no dialogue is possible. Dialogue presupposes that the truth can be sought, acquired, and shared, that logos is the basis of dia-logos” (109).

But here we come to another statement by Cardinal Vesco that I find problematic. He does not just reject attempts to convert; he does not think we should even have interreligious dialogue with Muslims. When asked what the conditions for fruitful dialogue with Muslims would be, he answered flatly: “My deep conviction is that dialogue should not take place on the religious level. It is not Christian–Muslim dialogue that will improve the situation in the banlieues.” To give him the benefit of the doubt, perhaps he means that there are too many obstacles to dialogue on the religious level that need to be removed before any such thing could be attempted in Algeria. But, as stated, the cardinal says we ought not try to convert people to Christianity and that we ought not even engage in interreligious dialogue with Muslims. Neither exemplify the Catholic position.

Let me conclude with words from Nostra Aetate regarding the Catholic view of our relation to other religions, including Islam: “The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions. . . . However [vero], she proclaims, and ever must proclaim Christ ‘the way, the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6), in whom men may find the fullness of religious life” (2, emphasis added).

items.title: Stop Cheapening Human Dignity with Partisan Politics
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Beyond the general imperative not to harm people and to do what’s possible to care for those in need, human dignity, by itself, does not have much to say about what we should and should not do in the political realm.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

The atheist public intellectual, Steven Pinker, penned an influential essay nearly twenty years ago entitled, “The Stupidity of Dignity.” Pinker argues that appeals to human dignity are “squishy” and “subjective” and fail to support “the heavyweight moral demands assigned to it.” He prefers “autonomy” as an alternative. 

Autonomy, however, is also subjective and squishy. Indeed, from a purely materialist atheistic perspective, we can’t coherently claim that autonomy exists because it’s not “matter.” Using autonomy to justify morality also means—unsettlingly—that babies, the elderly, the mentally and physically impaired, and, if we’re consistent, those who are asleep have little or no value because they are not fully autonomous. 

Autonomy thus has trouble supporting the moral weight assigned to it too. 

Yet Pinker remains right that human dignity is often misused as a catch-all justification. Like “diversity,” “inclusion,” and “social justice,” appeals to dignity frequently assume that the meaning of the term is self-evident and that its very utterance establishes the moral supremacy of the position it’s advancing. 

Pinker’s critique was aimed at dignity’s use in bioethics. However, invocations of dignity are also prominent in contemporary foreign policy and immigration debates. Why, for example, is it wrong to question indiscriminately sending money to international NGOs? Because it’s an offense to human dignity. Why should we never challenge the constitutionality of birth citizenship? Because it’s an offense to human dignity (an “offense” currently committed by every country in Europe, none of which recognizes American-style birth citizenship). Why must we remain silent about the harms caused by mass migration? Because it’s an offense against human dignity. Why should the national census—which determines political representation—include illegal aliens? Because failing to do so, yes, is an offense against human dignity. 

And how does dignity lead to these conclusions?

Because it does. 

The tragedy is that human dignity, rightly defined, should form the foundation of the moral and political order. To recognize dignity is simply to affirm that all human beings have inherent and equal worth merely by virtue of being human. 

Defined this way, human dignity generates two kinds of moral imperatives: (1) negative prohibitions (things we should not do) and (2) positive mandates (things we should do). What’s prohibited? Everything that, until recently, everyone in the West believed was wrong; for example, murder, mutilation, abuse, torture, false imprisonment, theft, and exploitation. What’s mandated? Caring for those unable to care for themselves. 

But here’s the crucial point: the only way to respect the negative prohibitions that human dignity generates is not to act—not to kill the innocent, not to mutilate, not to abuse, not to imprison without just cause, not to take what’s not yours, not to take advantage of others, etc.

What about the mandate to care for those in need? Like the negative prohibition, the moral imperative itself is categorical: all things being equal, we should take care of those who cannot care for themselves. Yet there is a crucial distinction: while there’s only one way to respect the negative prohibition on violating human dignity (not doing it), there are manifold ways to respect human dignity by providing aid. 

A host of questions arises: Whose needs should I focus on and in what order of importance? What is the most effective method of giving assistance? What may appear to be helpful but is actually harmful? How can I provide aid in a way that does not cause an injustice to another, including my own family, community, and country? How can I be sure that the need is authentic and not fraudulent? How do I respond when those receiving aid appear to be taking advantage of it? How do I respond when those receiving aid are using it to cause harm to themselves or to others?  

The complexity rises exponentially when the “I” becomes a “we” in the form of government policy, especially when recognizing that public expenditure to assist the needy comes from public funds, which come from taxation and are backed by the coercive power of the state. Respecting people’s dignity in the form of giving them something—especially if that something includes the benefits of citizenship—thus quickly becomes a highly contested political question, one that can only be addressed by wading through a sea of competing moral assertions based on an incomplete and often distorted understanding of the causes and effects of the problems we are seeking to address.    

The point is that, beyond the general imperative not to harm people and to do what’s possible to care for those in need, human dignity, by itself, does not have much to say about what we should and should not do in the political realm. This is not a criticism of human dignity. It is only a recognition of its moral and political limits. 

To identify these limits, however, is to criticize those who engage in the rhetorical abuse of dignity, those who brazenly and carelessly toss it about in political discourse as both a weapon to advance their aims and as a shield from scrutiny. The end result—and I fear we’re already there—is that “dignity” loses both its rhetorical and moral force, fading into just another word partisans employ to get what they want. 

A version of this article first appeared on the Washington Examiner.
